title: Python Foundations
description: Build a strong Python foundation before moving into data analysis tools and libraries.
objectives: Read and write Python using correct syntax, types, and indentation.
Write reusable functions with parameters, defaults, and return values.
Choose between a list and a dictionary for a given problem.
Read and write text and CSV files safely with the with statement.

slides.title: Python Foundations
slides.lead: Everything in this course — NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib — is built on plain Python. This module makes sure that base is solid.
bullets: Python Review — types, variables, control flow
Functions — package logic so you can reuse it
Lists & Dictionaries — the two containers you will use every day
File Handling — get data in and out of your program

slides.title: What you will be able to do
slides.lead: By the end of this module you should be comfortable doing all of the following without looking anything up.
bullets: Explain the difference between int, float, str, and bool
Write a function that takes arguments and returns a value
Loop over a list and over a dictionary's keys and values
Open a file, read its lines, and close it automatically
slides.note: If any bullet feels shaky at the end, revisit that topic before moving to Module 02.

slides.title: Variables and core types
slides.lead: Python is dynamically typed — a variable is just a name pointing at a value, and the value carries the type.
bullets: int — whole numbers: 42, -7
float — decimals: 3.14, 98.6
str — text in quotes: "Sokha"
bool — True or False
Use type(x) to check, int(x) / float(x) / str(x) to convert

slides.title: Control flow: if / for / while
slides.lead: Indentation is the syntax. Four spaces define a block — there are no braces.

body: for n in range(1, 4):      # 1, 2, 3  -> stop is excluded

slides.note: range(1, 4) gives 1, 2, 3 — the stop value is never included. This off-by-one catches everyone once.

slides.title: Strings you will actually use
slides.lead: Most real data arrives as messy text. These few string tools clean up the majority of it.
bullets: f-strings for formatting: f"{name} scored {score:.1f}"
.strip() — remove leading/trailing whitespace
.lower() / .upper() — normalise before comparing
.split(",") — turn one line into a list of fields
.replace(old, new) — swap out characters

body: city, country = [p.strip() for p in raw.strip().split(",")]

slides.title: Why functions
slides.lead: A function names a piece of logic so you can run it many times without repeating yourself.
bullets: def declares it, the name is how you call it
Parameters are inputs, return sends a value back
No return means the function returns None
Default values make arguments optional
Keep one function responsible for one job

body: """Return the mean of a list of numbers."""

slides.title: Arguments, defaults, and scope
slides.lead: Arguments can be passed by position or by name. Variables created inside a function do not leak outside it.

body: # print(status)  -> NameError: status only exists inside grade()

slides.note: Never use a mutable default like def f(items=[]) — the same list is shared across every call. Use None and create it inside.

slides.title: Practice: build three functions
slides.lead: Write these in a single .py file and test each one with at least two inputs.
bullets: celsius_to_fahrenheit(c) — return c * 9 / 5 + 32
is_passing(score, passing=50) — return True or False
summarise(scores) — return the count, min, max, and average as a dict

slides.title: Lists — ordered collections
slides.lead: A list holds items in order, indexed from 0, and can be changed after it is created.
bullets: Index from the front with [0], from the back with [-1]
Slice a range with [1:3] — stop is excluded
.append(x) adds one item, .extend([...]) adds many
len(), sum(), min(), max(), sorted() all work on lists
Loop with for item in items:

slides.title: Dictionaries — key to value
slides.lead: A dictionary looks things up by a key instead of a position. This is how a row of data is usually represented.
bullets: Create with {"key": value}, read with d["key"]
d.get("key", default) never raises KeyError
.keys(), .values(), .items() for looping
Assigning to a new key adds it
A list of dictionaries is effectively a table
slides.note: This student dict is one row. A list of these dicts is one table — which is exactly what a Pandas DataFrame wraps in Module 04.

slides.title: Putting them together
slides.lead: A list of dictionaries is the most common shape of raw data you will meet before Pandas.

body: avg = sum(s["score"] for s in students) / len(students)

slides.title: Reading and writing files
slides.lead: Always open files with the with statement — it closes the file for you, even if your code raises an error.
bullets: "r" read (default), "w" overwrite, "a" append
Always pass encoding="utf-8" so Khmer text survives
.read() gives one string, .readlines() gives a list
Looping over the file object reads line by line — best for big files
Lines keep their trailing \n — strip it

slides.title: CSV — the format your data will arrive in
slides.lead: The csv module reads a spreadsheet export into exactly the list-of-dictionaries shape from the last topic.

body: with open("students.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
row["score"] = float(row["score"])   # CSV values are always str

slides.note: Everything read from a CSV is a string. Converting types on the way in prevents a whole category of bugs later.

slides.title: Module 01 recap
slides.lead: You now have the vocabulary the rest of the course assumes.
bullets: Types and control flow — the grammar of Python
Functions — naming logic so it can be reused and tested
Lists and dictionaries — order versus lookup
Files — reading real data in with with open(...)
